cards.title: Visa, Mastercard, major banks facing new litigation over 'anticompetitive' fees

depth.text: a San Diego pizzeria is suing over **Visa and Mastercard’s** allegedly **inflated card fees**

The complaint alleges Visa and Mastercard worked with Bank of America, Capital One, Chase Bank, Citibank and Wells Fargo to set **uniform interchange fees**. It says their rules forced merchants to accept every card from either network and stopped them steering customers to **cheaper payment options**; the proposed class would cover US businesses and other entities that accepted those cards from **January 25, 2019** until the alleged effects end.

cards.camps: Two camps: some want merchants to steer customers toward cheaper payments or weaken card-network dominance; others say cards provide real value and question whether high fees alone make the market anticompetitive.

comments.text: I don't care about the fees as much as I care about the terrible experience of making payments. Why is it still such a chore to fill payment forms on the web? From the merchant side of things, they're paying about $0.60 to process the transaction via ACH, versus $2-$2.50 for credit card transactions, per fill-up. So…

Basic reforms that could solve this problem: 1. Merchants need to be allowed to add card processing fees on top of any transaction, and it should be possible to do this very easily. If not this, then any receipt should be required to include card processing fees. 2. Merchants should be allowed to pick and choose which cards they accept without penalty. Those two simple changes would add…

I do think we're getting to the point that middlemen don't have much value add. Economics even suggests they don't add value I think. Possibly neutral markets, payments, and logistics should just be a public service.

I wish they would face litigation for banning the sale of large swaths of content (or even banning the content altogether on sites relying on donations/subscriptions to survive). Paypros have no business being censors.

Kagan’s **1986 discovery** made a **greater excess of one mirror image** possible. Soai’s 2003 reaction formed only one of the two possible images, and their work helps chemists design reactions for **pharmaceuticals**.

depth.text: someone built a **tiny ad blocker** that searches **domain hashes** stored in flash instead of RAM
The **537k-domain “ultimate” list** only fits the single-app setup. Firmware OTA takes two app slots, leaving room for **~250k domains**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call the idea brilliant; others say its latency may be a deal breaker.

comments.text: Weird how the readme talks about hash collisions, but not in the way I would expect. Two blocked domains with the same hash isn't a problem, they both need to be blocked. Where hash collisions matter is false positives, e.g. if hash(google.com) = hash(adserver.com). There does appear to be a web dashboard and /unblock api so should be straightforward to resolve.

If you're ever thinking about getting an ESP32-C3, do yourself a favor and get the variant that you can connect an external antenna to. The normal C3 has a built-in antenna that is extremely weak, making it useless for most things I was planning using it for.

I'm a bit of a paranoid freak that likes lists, so I've got a PiHole that has a total list of 14-16M blocked domains. Great idea, and good for casual blocking, but I'm almost moving to an "allow list" mindset. This solution would probably work better for that, I wonder if the good parts of the internet would fit into an 140k list.
I think it could fit even more domains using a Bloom Filter or similar probabilistic data structure. With a chance of false-positives of course. But that's a trade-off the project already makes.

Whitelist/allowlist is easier, e.g., it's smaller Depends on the user but not everyone is visiting new websites everyday Even for those that are, the number of domain-IP mappings needed will be relatively small Definitely under 140,000 Most DNS data I use is "static", it rarely changes. cards.camps: Two camps: supporters welcome Chrome shipping JPEG XL; others point to compatibility gaps and question whether it beats AVIF.

cards.title: First enhanced geothermal power plant completed in just 23 months

depth.text: Fervo started selling **geothermal power** after Cape Station’s first block took **23 months** to build
Cape Station synchronized with the grid about a week ago, bringing online the first third of a planned **100-megawatt** plant. Fervo aims to finish future blocks in as little as **18 months**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the real news is Fervo’s progress in deep drilling; others question what “world’s first” means, pointing to earlier EGS projects.

comments.text:
The real news here is that Fervo has made progress in deep drilling.
Deep geothermal has been known for decades but almost nobody can get down there.
Fervo got down to 15,000 feet in 16 drilling days last year with a test well in Texas. 500F heat. That's where it gets useful. This new one is apparently not as deep but fans out with horizontal drilling.
Next step is presumably deep and horizontal…
They tried to drill for one in Switzerland twice. One in Basel and one in St. Gallen but both times causes earthquakes significant enough that the whole project was scraped.
Does "enhanced geothermal" have a definition beyond "drilling deeper", or "whatever anyone does that's different than what what was done before"?

23 months to build is impressive, but the number that matters for EGS is thermal drawdown. If the fractured rock cools faster than modeled they have to keep drilling new wells, so I'd like to see Cape's output a few years in.

If the coffin needed any more nails, this puts the final kibosh on that cancelled SMR project out there that centered on Utah and Idaho, the one involving NuScale. Geothermal makes much more sense for them now. There's a geothermal project at the Newberry Volcano in Oregon that also looks interesting (different people doing that).

I learned only recently that somebody is working on adding fluorescence to cuttlefish to see…

It's a rule in the Nobel Foundation's statutes added in 1968, a provision that no more than three persons may share a Nobel prize. In practice no science prize had gone to more than three people before that either. In medicine it usually means one or two key contributors get left out, as with Boyden and Bamberg this year.

glossary.hash collision: When two different inputs produce the same short fingerprint.
glossary.FNV-1a: A specific rule for turning data into a repeatable fingerprint.
glossary.binary search: A way to find something in a sorted list by checking the middle and narrowing the search repeatedly.
glossary.flash: Storage in a device that keeps information when the power is off.
glossary.PSRAM: Pseudo-static random-access memory: extra working space for a device's programs and data.
glossary.OTA: Over-the-air: sending an update to a device through its network connection.
glossary.Bloom filter: A compact way to check whether something is on a list; it can sometimes say yes when it isn't.
glossary.Unique Games Conjecture: A claim about limits on how closely quick computer methods can solve certain problems.
glossary.Lean certificate: A proof written in a format a computer can check step by step.
glossary.NP-hard: A label for problems at least as hard as the toughest problems whose answers can be checked quickly.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.lawful access: A proposed legal power to make online services help authorities monitor people or get information.
glossary.CSIS: Canadian Security Intelligence Service: Canada's intelligence agency.
glossary.encryption: A way of scrambling information so only someone with the right key can read it.
glossary.backdoor: A way into a protected device or service that bypasses its normal security.
glossary.mirrors: Copies of software or files kept on different computers so people can get them from another place.
glossary.YAML: A readable text format for writing settings and instructions in a structured way.
glossary.Docker CLI plugin: A small add-on you can run by typing a Docker command in a terminal.
glossary.MCP server: Model Context Protocol server: a computer that lets an AI connect to outside tools or information.
glossary.orchestration: Coordinating several AI agents so they can hand tasks to one another.
glossary.agent harness: The surrounding software that runs an AI agent and helps manage its work.
glossary.JavaScript: A programming language; here, it lets an agent combine tool calls.
glossary.DMCA takedown notice: Digital Millennium Copyright Act: a notice asking a website to remove material that someone says copies their work.
glossary.§ 1201: A section of US law that one commenter says prohibits getting around a tool that controls access to copyrighted material.
glossary.copyright infringement: Using somebody else's protected work in a way copyright law doesn't permit.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.calibration: How well a model’s confidence matches how often its choices are actually right.
glossary.pointer head: A part of Jeeves that scores answer options to produce probabilities.
glossary.LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation: a way to adapt an AI for a new task by training a small add-on instead of changing the whole AI.
glossary.NPU: Neural Processing Unit: a chip part made to handle the kinds of calculations used by AI.
glossary.JevBench: A collection of questions used to compare how accurately models answer and how well their confidence matches.
glossary.burnout: A state of exhaustion that happens when work drains more energy than it gives back.
glossary.AI brainfry: Feeling mentally overloaded from running AI agents in parallel.
glossary.selection bias: A comparison gets skewed because the people included are different from the people left out.
glossary.tech debt: Extra cleanup work left behind when software choices make future changes harder.
glossary.IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol: a way for a mail app to read and sync messages kept by an email service.
glossary.POP3: Post Office Protocol version 3: a way for a mail app to fetch messages from an email service.
glossary.SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the system mail apps use to send messages.
glossary.CalDAV: Calendaring Extensions to WebDAV: a way for calendar apps to share and sync calendars.
glossary.CardDAV: vCard Extensions to WebDAV: a way for apps to share and sync contacts.
glossary.Sieve: A way to write rules that automatically sort or handle incoming email.
glossary.GnuPG: GNU Privacy Guard: a tool for signing messages so others can check who sent them, or encrypting them so only intended people can read them.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.GPL-3.0-or-later: A software licence that lets people use, change, and share software under its terms.
glossary.JMAP: JSON Meta Application Protocol: a way for mail apps to exchange email with a mail service.
glossary.WebView: A browser built into another app, used to show web content.
glossary.tracking pixel: A tiny, often hidden image that can tell a sender when an email was opened.
glossary.Flatpak: A way to install Linux apps in packages that include many of the pieces they need.
glossary.MIME: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions: rules email uses to carry attachments and different kinds of content.
glossary.UUID: Universally unique identifier: a label designed to identify one item without being confused with another.
glossary.mbox: A file format that stores many email messages together.
glossary.maildir: A way to store each email as its own file in a folder.
glossary.sandboxing: Restricting what a program can access so it cannot freely affect the rest of the system.
glossary.vibe-coded: Made by steering an AI with informal requests instead of writing most of the code by hand.
glossary.PETSCII: PET Standard Code of Information Interchange: the Commodore's set of letters and symbols, including graphics.
glossary.webfont: A font made to load on a website, so its text can use that lettering.
glossary.keycap: The top of a keyboard key, where its letter or symbol is printed.
glossary.decoding: Turning the data in an image file into a picture a browser can show.
glossary.lossless compression: Making an image file smaller without losing any of the original image information.
glossary.HDR: High Dynamic Range: a way for a screen to show more detail in bright and dark areas.
glossary.SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: a way to apply one operation to several values at once.
glossary.progressive decoding: Showing an image bit by bit as it loads, instead of waiting for the full image.
glossary.Lean proof: A proof checked by Lean, a program that helps catch gaps in mathematical reasoning.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.beta: A version released for people to try before it is considered finished.
glossary.predicate: A check asking whether something is true, with an estimate of how likely that is.
glossary.rubric: A set of rules for judging or scoring something.
glossary.calibrated: A model is calibrated when its confidence matches how often its answers are right.
glossary.antitrust: Rules meant to stop companies from becoming so powerful that they can squeeze out competition.
glossary.sovereign wealth fund: A fund a government invests public money in, often to support spending or save for the future.
glossary.non-voting shares: Ownership in a company that doesn't give the holder a vote on company decisions.
glossary.biomass: The combined mass of living things in a species or group.
glossary.carbon mass: The weight of just the carbon in living things, not everything they are made of.
glossary.perennial: A plant whose root system stays alive between harvests.
glossary.clonal colony: A group of trees that share connected roots and grow as one organism.
glossary.relinker: A tool that changes a program into the format another system expects.
glossary.system PRX libraries: PS5 system code that games expect to use; this project supplies its own versions.
glossary.emulation: Software that imitates an operation a chip cannot do directly, so the program can still run.
glossary.dynamic linking: A program using a separate piece of code while it runs, instead of having that code built in.
glossary.SPIR-V: A format for the graphics instructions produced by the project's shader recompiler.
glossary.Vulkan: A way for software to send graphics work to a graphics card.
glossary.x86-64: A kind of computer code understood by many PC processors.
glossary.GNM command buffers: Batches of drawing instructions a game sends for the PlayStation to carry out.
glossary.desktop wrapper: A program that packages a website or browser app so it can run like a desktop app.
glossary.cleanroom: A way to build software by studying what it does while keeping its original code out of the process.
glossary.OSS: Open-source software: software whose code is shared so others can inspect it and sometimes reuse it under a license.
glossary.preference signals: Clues from people's choices that can help show what answers they prefer.
glossary.context: A value passed along with work so it can carry a stop signal or a timeout.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.reward hacking: When an AI finds a way to get a high score without doing what its designers actually wanted.
glossary.chain of thought: A written-out account of an AI's reasoning; it may not show the process that actually led to its answer.
glossary.Schelling point: A choice that separate people can settle on independently because they expect others to choose it too.
glossary.egregore: A group made of many parts that seems to act as its own entity and pursue its own goals.
glossary.RL: Reinforcement Learning: a way to teach an AI by rewarding actions that get the desired result.
glossary.enhanced geothermal: A way to generate electricity by drilling down to hot rock deeper underground.
glossary.EGS: Enhanced Geothermal System: a method for drawing heat from deep underground rock to make electricity.
glossary.grid: The network that carries electricity from power stations to the places that use it.
glossary.thermal drawdown: How quickly the underground rock cools as a plant draws heat from it.
glossary.hyperscalers: Very large companies that run huge data centres and rent computing power to other businesses.
glossary.optogenetics: A way to use light to control nerve cells, so researchers can test what those cells do.
glossary.channelrhodopsins: Proteins that make cells respond to light, so light can switch their activity.
glossary.vectors: Carriers researchers use to get genetic instructions into cells.
glossary.MTA: Material Transfer Agreement: paperwork that sets the rules for sharing research materials.
glossary.action potentials: Brief electrical signals nerve cells use to pass messages.
glossary.PI: Principal investigator: the main scientist leading a research project.
